notes.meaning: Agur speaks here as an inspired teacher delivering a solemn message to his companions, Ithiel and Ucal. He begins his message by expressing his own deep weariness and human limitation before God. Recognising our personal weakness is the first step toward depending entirely on the Lord.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read the Hebrew text as a cry of human exhaustion ('I am weary, O God, and worn out') rather than seeing Ithiel and Ucal as names of people.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The traditional Latin Vulgate translated the Hebrew names as descriptive titles, rendering the phrase as 'The words of the gatherer, the son of the vomiter.'

notes.meaning: Agur confesses that on his own, he lacks the basic wisdom and understanding that a person should have. He never went to human schools of philosophy, and he cannot grasp the holy things of God by his own strength. A person must admit their own ignorance before they can receive God's wisdom.

A series of questions challenges anyone to name a mortal man who has traveled to heaven, held the wind in his hands, or set the boundaries of the earth. Only God rules the universe like this, so no mere human can claim equal knowledge with Him. The mysterious question about God's Son hints at the divine Person through whom God creates and governs all things.

differ.view: Matthew Henry teaches that this verse clearly points forward to the Messiah as a divine Person distinct from the Father, whose name was kept hidden until the gospel revealed Him.
Adam Clarke cautions that readers should not use this obscure verse to prove the doctrine of the Trinity, arguing that essential doctrines should only be defended with clear, unmistakable passages.
John Gill sees this as a direct Old Testament revelation of God's eternal Son, who shares the exact nature and power of the Father as a distinct person.

notes.meaning: Every word God gives is completely pure and reliable, like gold that has been refined in a hot furnace. The Lord acts as a protective shield for all who put their trust in what He has said. Therefore, no one should dare to add human traditions or false teachings to Scripture, because God will expose such people as liars.

Agur asks God for two specific favors to guide his daily life until he dies. First, he asks to be kept far away from dishonesty, false teachings, and vain pursuits. Second, he asks for neither poverty nor great wealth, but just enough food for each day. He fears that having too much might make him proud and forget God, while being desperately poor might tempt him to steal and bring shame to God's holy name.

An earnest warning tells readers never to slander or falsely accuse a servant to their master. Adding to the troubles of someone already in a lowly position is unjust and cruel. When the mistreated servant appeals to God for justice, God will hold the accuser guilty.

Agur describes two awful kinds of people that can ruin a society. The first kind are children who show vile ingratitude by cursing their fathers and refusing to speak kindly to their mothers. The second kind are self-righteous people who think they are morally clean, yet they remain stained with hidden, unconfessed sin.

Two more wicked groups of people are brought into view. One group is filled with intolerable pride, showing their arrogance by looking down on everyone else with contempt. The next group consists of greedy oppressors whose words and actions act like sharp swords, devouring the poor and needy from the land.

The blood-sucking leech is pictured with two daughters who never stop crying out for more. This image introduces four things in the world that never say they have had enough: the grave that swallows the dead, the childless womb that longs for children, parched land that drinks in rain, and blazing fire that consumes all fuel. Selfish greed and sinful appetite are just as hard to satisfy.

A grim warning describes the fate of a child who rolls their eyes in mockery at their parents. Those who treat their father and mother with open disdain often face a violent, shameful end, left unburied like carrion for ravens and young vultures to eat. God will not let rebellious disrespect toward parents go unpunished.

Four things are singled out as too deep and marvelous for the human mind to fully track. An eagle flies through the open air without leaving a visible trail, a snake slides smoothly over a solid rock, a ship crosses the open sea without marking the water permanently, and a man wins the heart of a young woman. Each of these shows a mysterious path that cannot be easily measured.

The mysterious ways just described also illustrate the crafty behavior of an unfaithful woman. She commits her secret sin, wipes her mouth just like someone finishing an ordinary meal, and casually insists she has done nothing wrong. Her hardened conscience allows her to hide her guilt from other people.

Society shakes and groans when people obtain power or positions that their character cannot handle. Four examples are given: a slave who becomes a king and turns into a tyrant, a crude fool who grows wealthy and overbearing, a bitter and unloved woman whose marriage only makes her haughty, and a servant girl who replaces her mistress and acts proudly. Sudden honor without humility always causes distress.

True wisdom does not depend on physical size or bodily strength, as seen in four of God's smallest creatures. Ants are tiny and weak, yet they show great wisdom by gathering their food in summer to prepare for the future. Rock badgers are frail animals with little defenses, yet they display good sense by making safe homes high up in the rocky cliffs.

Locusts have no leader or king over them, yet they move forward together in orderly ranks and accomplish great things through unity. Lizards are small enough to be picked up in a person's hand, yet through quiet skill and persistence they make their homes in royal palaces. God wants His people to learn unity, patience, and diligence from these lowly creatures.

Agur names four examples of beings that move with dignity, strength, and confidence. The lion is the mightiest of beasts and refuses to turn back before any danger, the strutting rooster or fleet greyhound carries itself with grace, the he-goat marches boldly at the head of the flock, and a king walks with undisputed authority among his troops. Believers should show similar boldness and steadfastness when doing what is right.

Anyone who has acted foolishly by boasting of their own importance, or who has planned evil against another person, should immediately cover their mouth in silence. Churning whole milk produces butter, and punching or twisting a nose makes it bleed, showing that forcing anger will always stir up quarrels. Choosing to be silent and humble stops a fight before it ever starts.
